title: J0754 archival observations and physical interpretation
subtitle: Research report for scientific review  |  8 November 2026
credit: Prepared with Kyle using AI-assisted analysis by Ari and contributions from Gemini Argon. Public telescope observations retain their original survey attribution. This report has not been peer reviewed or submitted.

pages.title: The star and its long term brightness changes
sections: Principal result

DASCH J075445.9+164141 shows a modern multi-year fading and recovery independently recorded by ZTF and ASAS-SN, accompanied by smaller infrared changes in NEOWISE. A flare-like TESS event and recurring roughly 36-day modulation add direct evidence relevant to an active, rotating giant. Changing starspots, potentially sustained by a close companion, are our leading working interpretation. The observations establish the variability and activity evidence; they do not yet establish the mechanism of the long dimming.
Identity and prior work

The target is Gaia DR3 667401913089980544, TIC 18878735, 2MASS J07544588+1641407, ASAS J075446+1641.7 and ASASSN-V J075445.83+164141.1. The working ICRS position is RA 118.6911741 degrees, Dec +16.6946212 degrees. Tang et al. (2010) identified its unusual historical fading and a K2III-like spectrum with chromospheric Ca II H and K emission [1]. This is a follow-up of that known variable, not a new star discovery. A 2011 poster gives an atmosphere fit near 4500 K; Gaia supplies a hotter solution near 5206 K. Model-dependent quantities below state which baseline was adopted.
Modern optical and infrared measurements

ZTF differential g photometry gives +0.3089 mag fading from 2018 to 2022 and -0.1393 mag recovery from 2022 to 2025. Independent ASAS-SN g cameras give +0.285 to +0.313 mag fading; five camera streams support recovery, continuing into 2026. The original ASAS-SN file contains 5,249 rows, of which 5,180 V and g observations pass the retained quality rule. Filters and cameras are analyzed separately. ZTF contributes 470 quality-passing target observations and 364 same-exposure differential measurements. Agreement across surveys and cameras strongly reduces the likelihood of a single-survey artifact (Figure 1).

Comparison-corrected NEOWISE annual visit medians fade by +0.1163 mag in W1 (3.4 microns) and +0.0894 mag in W2 (4.6 microns), then partly recover through the last target visit in March 2024. The March matched-state contrasts used for modeling are g +0.312, W1 +0.1175 and W2 +0.08875 mag: approximately 25.0%, 10.3% and 7.8% flux loss. Matching optical observations within 30 days of infrared visits gives g-W1 reddening of approximately 0.19-0.22 mag. This is an optical-to-infrared color change; no validated contemporaneous g-r curve was recovered (Figure 2).
Historical extension

The retained DASCH series contains 552 differential detections from 1892 to 1989. The 1930s event survives the comparison-star and quality tests, with an event-to-baseline contrast near +0.68 mag in the photographic system. Only three retained points in 1892-1893 describe the proposed earlier dip. Legacy ASAS observations fill part of the later gap: exact-frame ensemble correction gives +0.147 mag fading from 2004 to 2007 and -0.114 mag recovery by 2009. Leaving out individual controls retains the fading. APPLAUSE plate and pixel tests remain inconclusive. Different passbands and sparse historical coverage prevent treating the episodes as identical eclipses or measuring a long recurrence period (Figure 3).

pages.title: The TESS flare and evidence of stellar activity
sections: The 2021 December 23 event

TESS sector 46 records a roughly 2.5% brightening with a rapid rise and slower decay, a measured full width at half maximum of 4.61 hours, and a tail extending roughly ten hours. We examined extracted light curves and the native calibrated 7 by 7 pixel TESSCut cube, containing 3,707 cadences at approximately ten-minute sampling. The compact positive difference-image excess lies 0.177 pixel, or about 3.7 arcseconds, from the Gaia position projected into the image. A spatial-derivative sensitivity fit does not explain the excursion as pointing motion alone. These results support a stellar flare associated with J0754 (Figure 4).
Radiated energy

Integrating the fractional excess gives an equivalent duration of 601 seconds. Nine baseline and integration-window combinations span 518-780 seconds; trapezoidal integration bridges one approximately 50-minute gap. Using the actual TESS response, a 9000 K flare blackbody, stellar temperature 5206 K and luminosity 54.6 solar luminosities gives 5.3 x 10^37 erg under a face-on, optically thick surface-patch convention. The corresponding isotropic-equivalent energy is 2.1 x 10^38 erg. The factor of four reflects different emission geometries and must not be treated as two independent measurements.

Varying stellar luminosity from 30 to 60 solar luminosities, stellar temperature from 4500 to 5250 K, flare temperature from 8000 to 12000 K and the baseline/window choices gives a surface-patch energy envelope of 2.1 x 10^37 to 1.25 x 10^38 erg. This is a model-sensitivity range, not a confidence interval. Under the adopted host association the event lies comfortably in the superflare regime. The localization has no formal PRF-calibrated astrometric error model, so an unresolved neighboring host remains a material alternative. This host and spectral assumption is the principal qualification on the energy.
Optical flare profile comparison

Peak- and width-normalized overlays compare the event with the empirical Davenport et al. (2014) optical stellar-flare template and a published solar white-light profile [2,3]. J0754 has the expected broad fast-rise, slow-decay morphology, with differences in its rise and tail. The solar curve was approximately digitized from a published figure; the stellar curve uses the published template equations. This is a shape comparison, not a statistical template fit or evidence that the Sun and this giant release the same energy (Figure 5).
Swift and FAST observations

The public 2SXPS source J075445.6+164139 (catalogue ID 161839) lies 3.88 arcseconds from J0754, within its 5.6-arcsecond 90% positional radius. The catalogue reports 18 counts and 4,183 seconds effective exposure. A 1 keV thermal-plasma conversion with NH = 4.34 x 10^20 cm^-2 and distance 1668 pc gives unabsorbed Lx approximately 4.2 x 10^31 erg/s. The two useful 2009 December 2 snapshot bins do not resolve a flare; their constancy test has p = 0.141. The Swift observation and the 2021 TESS flare are separate events, twelve years apart [4].

Ten FAST extracted spectra cover eight nights in 2008-2012. H-alpha absorption pseudo-equivalent width falls from approximately 1.32 Angstrom in October 2008 to 0.84 Angstrom on 2009 November 12, a 0.480 +/- 0.085 Angstrom formal-noise contrast. It survives the tested resolution and continuum variants, but a 1.675% differential continuum bias could reproduce its size. Registered native line profiles show no convincing detached blueshifted absorption identifying erupting gas. Broad Mg and Na indices supply no precise temperature change. Together with Tang's established Ca H/K emission, the new observations support an active-star interpretation without identifying a single flare precursor (Figure 6).

pages.title: Rotation companion evidence and changing modulation
sections: A recurring roughly 36 day timescale

We searched periods from 10 to 100 days in the retained daily optical measurements. Each July-June observing season has independent sine and cosine coefficients, allowing its phase and amplitude to change. Camera offsets and within-camera linear trends are fitted jointly with the oscillation. Seasons require at least 30 daily camera groups and 120 days span. ASAS-SN provides nine qualifying seasons; independent ZTF differential photometry provides six. The equal-season mean fractional residual-variance improvement peaks at 35.78 days in ASAS-SN and 36.30 days in ZTF (Figure 7).

Eight of nine ASAS-SN seasonal maxima fall between 34.1 and 37.3 days; five of six ZTF maxima fall between 35.4 and 37.3 days. Both surveys show a weak exact-period component in 2024/25. Shared-camera block-sign diagnostics with 3, 7 and 14 day blocks produce no combined peak as large as observed in 256 draws for either survey. These are correlated-noise sensitivity checks, not calibrated false-alarm probabilities. The recurring timescale in two surveys supports rotation of a spotted star; the difference between seasonal peaks is not a measured differential-rotation rate.
What the earlier failed fit actually tested

The previous test held the exact 35.92046-day waveform fixed across years. Freezing the pre-2022 waveform worsens later ASAS-SN squared prediction error by 26%; ZTF worsens by about 63%. That excludes this stable waveform as a description of the later photometry. It does not exclude the recurring timescale recovered when each season can change phase. Separately, the 912.3-day ASAS-SN catalogue period fails modern waveform-replay and blocked/forward tests. Fits spanning less than a full long cycle do not establish a replacement multi-year period.
Amplitude versus the long dip

The rotational swing does not increase monotonically as the star fades. In bright 2019/20, fixed-period peak-to-peak amplitudes are 0.050 mag (ASAS-SN) and 0.056 mag (ZTF). Near the faint state in 2022/23 they are 0.046 and 0.056 mag. During recovery in 2024/25 they fall to 0.010 and 0.0048 mag; ASAS-SN rises again to 0.038 mag in 2025/26. Allowing the previously selected nearby seasonal periods gives descriptive brightness-amplitude rank correlations near zero in both surveys. Rotational amplitude measures the asymmetry of surface brightness around the star, not total spotted area (Figure 8).
Shorter stretches during 2024/25

At the fixed 35.92046-day period, early 120-day fits recover peak-to-peak amplitudes of 0.036 mag in ASAS-SN and 0.032 mag in ZTF, substantially above the whole-season values. Two calendar halves split on 2025 January 15 give early amplitudes of 0.033 and 0.025 mag. Later ASAS-SN modulation weakens; sparse ZTF data suggest phase changes with weaker correlated-noise support. Ninety-day sensitivity windows show the same broad change. The season-long fit therefore hides some within-season modulation. Amplitude evolution, phase evolution and a slightly different period remain confounded; no particular spot lifetime is measured.
Gaia companion candidate

Gaia DR3 publishes an SB1 solution with period 35.9205 +/- 0.0306 days, radial-velocity semi-amplitude 10.72 +/- 0.81 km/s and 21 good velocities. Eccentricity 0.023 +/- 0.056 is consistent with zero. Its efficiency 0.189 and significance 13.31 fall below the processing team's recommended gold-sample thresholds [5]. Individual Gaia epoch velocities are unavailable for an independent refit. The catalogue supports a close-companion candidate. Agreement with the photometric rotation timescale makes tidal maintenance of activity plausible, while orbital confirmation and synchronization remain open.

pages.title: Physical models archive limits and conclusions
sections: Testing spots against the wavelength changes

CK04 stellar atmospheres integrated through public filter responses reproduce the main three-band changes with a two-temperature, fixed-area spot model [6]. An illustrative 5000 K photosphere with approximately 3650 K spots increases projected spot coverage from 30% to 49.6%. Fitting g and W1 gives changes of +0.312 and +0.1167 mag; the unused W2 prediction is +0.0995 mag versus +0.08875 observed. The 0.011-mag residual is inside the adopted 0.02-mag model tolerance. The coverage and temperature are an example solution, not measured surface properties. Other starting coverages also fit. The color/amplitude test demonstrates feasibility, not unique model selection (Figure 9).
Competing mechanisms and infrared spectra

Ordinary uniform foreground dust screens normalized to a 0.30-mag optical fade predict only about 0.013-0.015 mag at W1 and 0.007-0.009 mag at W2, far below the observed infrared fading. Pure single-component gray fading also fails. Partial covering, temperature plus geometric scale, two-component dilution and some atmosphere-grid cooling cases remain viable. Fits to two training bands with two adjustable parameters cannot select the cause.

We recovered 223 SPHEREx spectral-image overlaps in October 2025 and April 2026; 182 local measurements pass the extraction rule. The official IRSA tool independently reduced the same pixels, with detector median native/local flux ratios 0.966-1.028. Fitting the 0.75-2.4 micron spectrum accounts for most of the observed 2.45-5 micron continuum. An approximately 9% April long-wave residual remains sensitive to atmosphere and calibration choices. No dominant warm infrared emitter is required by this check; a small excess or cold obscuring material is not ruled out. These are recovery-era spectra, not observations at the 2022 minimum (Figure 10).
Negative results and archive coverage

Independent APPLAUSE confirmation of the historical event remains inconclusive. Saturation limits PS1, UHS and most PTF points; synthetic PS1 mean values were not accepted as observed colors. LAMOST spectra have zero or invalid continua. Gaia XP supplies broad mean-spectrum context, not an epoch temperature/RV series. GALEX adds one secure near-UV measurement, insufficient to diagnose a hot component. Catalina has image coverage without recovered target photometry; NSVS catalogue coverage did not yield its time series. Other bounded archive searches added no usable constraint. Empty catalogue searches were not converted into upper limits.

An illustrative dusty-cloud budget can produce a 25% occultation with about 1.45 x 10^21 g under adopted opacity assumptions, but free lateral expansion at 1 km/s over eight years increases the required area by roughly 1700 times. No gas-ejection, dust-formation or confinement model has been demonstrated. The 2021 flare occurs after the modern fading began, so it cannot initiate the 2018 decline. No detached H-alpha outflow was identified. Neither the cloud calculation nor a lack of blueshift establishes the dimming mechanism.
Conclusion and review priorities

The central result is a magnetically active giant with independently replicated multi-year fading, a localized TESS superflare candidate and recurring roughly 36-day modulation. Evolving spots, possibly maintained by a close companion, provide a physically viable interpretation of the optical-infrared changes. We have not established that activity causes the long dip. The highest-value independent checks are multi-epoch radial velocities, calibrated temperature/activity spectra and matched optical/near-infrared colors. Our extracted measurements and scripts are provided for review. Novelty of the 2021 event needs a catalogue/event-level literature check before a priority claim.

[3] Hao et al. 2017 solar white-light profile, pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5736556/. [4] Swift 2SXPS source J075445.6+164139, swift.ac.uk/2SXPS/. [5] Gaia DR3 SB1 processing, arxiv.org/abs/2410.14372, and the official NSS data model. [6] STScI CK04 atmospheres, SVO Filter Profile Service and Draine dust models. Native archive links and input hashes are retained in the supporting packet. Analyses preserve stated quality cuts, camera/filter identities and comparison-star tests. Formal errors and illustrative sensitivity envelopes are distinguished from calibrated detection confidence. The appendix captions identify superseded or diagnostic figures; the packet includes machine-readable results, source scripts and an inventory of locally retained native files.
